```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 150, out.width = "100%")
```

An age adjusted rate is a weighted average of age specific rates. When all
age groups share a trend, the average describes each of them. When they do
not, it can hide opposite movements: colorectal cancer incidence, for
example, has been falling in older adults and rising in younger adults, and
the age adjusted rate for all ages mostly reflects the older age groups,
where rates are highest.

Analyzing every age group separately is the opposite extreme: many noisy
series, many tests. Multi-group clustering finds the middle ground. It partitions contiguous age groups into clusters
whose trends are as parallel as possible within a cluster and different
between clusters, then fits one model to the age adjusted rate of each
cluster.

## A known truth

To see whether clustering finds the right answer, we simulate incidence
counts for eight ten year age groups over 1990 to 2019. The four younger
groups rise steadily by 2% per year; the four older groups rise by 1% per
year until 2005 and fall by 3% per year afterwards.

```{r}
library(joinpoint)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(2026)
ages <- sprintf("%02d-%02d", seq(0, 70, 10), seq(9, 79, 10))
sim <- expand.grid(year = 1990:2019, age = ages, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
older <- match(sim$age, ages) > 4
log_rate <- log(2) + 0.35 * match(sim$age, ages) +
  ifelse(older, 0.01 * (sim$year - 1990) - 0.04 * pmax(sim$year - 2005, 0),
         0.02 * (sim$year - 1990))
sim$population <- 1e7
sim$count <- rpois(nrow(sim), exp(log_rate) * 100)
```

## The age adjusted rate hides the divergence

`age_adjust()` computes directly standardized rates and their standard
errors. Here the 2000 United States standard population, up to age 79, is
collapsed into the same ten year groups.

```{r, fig.alt = "Simulated age adjusted incidence rate by year, 1990 to 2019, with the fitted joinpoint model: a rise, one joinpoint, then a decline."}
us <- subset(std_populations, standard == "us2000")[1:17, ]
grp <- c(rep(ages[1], 3), rep(ages[-1], each = 2))
data.frame(us$age_group, grp)[c(1:4, 16:17), ]
std <- tapply(us$population, grp, sum)
aa <- age_adjust(sim, year, count, population, age, std)
fit_all <- joinpoint(aa, year, rate, se = se, kmax = 2,
                     ci_method = "parametric")
autoplot(fit_all) + labs(y = "Age adjusted rate per 100,000")
```

The all ages trend shows one turning point and a decline, the story of the
older groups. The steady rise in younger people is invisible.

## Clustering the age groups

`jp_cluster()` runs the whole algorithm: it compresses sparse age groups,
fits parallel joinpoint models to every block of contiguous groups, finds
the best partition for each number of clusters, selects the number of
clusters by BIC, and fits the final models to the age adjusted rates of
each cluster.

```{r}
cl <- jp_cluster(sim, year, count, population, age, std, kmax = 2,
                 ci_method = "parametric")
cl$selection[, c("clusters", "Q", "bic", "selected", "partition")]
cl$clusters
```

The BIC selects two clusters, 0 to 39 and 40 to 79 years, which is the truth
of the simulation. The final fits recover the two trends:

```{r, fig.alt = "Age adjusted rates of the two clusters of age groups by year, with their fitted joinpoint models and the APC of each segment with its confidence interval: a steady rise in one cluster and a rise followed by a decline in the other."}
autoplot(cl$fit, labels = "ci") + labs(y = "Age adjusted rate per 100,000")
```

When the differences between neighboring clusters are too small to be of
interest, the clustering MADWD (`madwd`, in percentage points) reduces the
number of clusters until every pair of adjacent clusters differs by at
least that much on average.
